# CHAPTER 1 THE PROBLEM AND ITS BACKGROUND
## PROJECT CONTEXT
Cognitive load is the mental effort required by a task, drawing on an individual's limited processing capacity [1], [2]. This concept is central to ergonomics and human factors, as mental demands are strongly associated with performance and safety in complex tasks [3]. With the increasing complexity of digital systems and technology-driven environments, monitoring cognitive load has become increasingly important in domains such as education, healthcare, transportation, and human–computer interaction. In this study, cognitive load is used as a label for task conditions: COLET's easiest activity (A1) counts as low load, and its hardest activity, which adds counting aloud under time pressure (A4), counts as high load. Related terms used by other studies, such as mental workload and mental effort, are treated as the same idea.

Current approaches for measuring cognitive load mainly utilize subjective questionnaires such as the NASA-Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) [4] or physiological measures like electroencephalography and cardiac activity [5]. Such questionnaires are administered after tasks and depend on participants’ self-assessment of their effort, while different workload efforts may produce inconsistent results [6]. Physiological sensors require highly specialized and professional equipment which may be intrusive and are difficult to deploy outside controlled environments, while eye tracking provides a less intrusive alternative that records pupil size, blinks, fixations, and saccades during task performance. This study uses data from a head-mounted tracker; remote and webcam-based trackers are left for future work. A systematic review of 91 studies demonstrated that several eye-tracking measures are responsive to changes in mental workload, with pupil diameter significant in 79% of the studies that measured it, fixation duration in 73%, and blink rate in 71% [5].

Machine learning enables the integration of eye-tracking measures into models that classify cognitive load levels. Logistic Regression, a linear model, provides interpretable coefficients that indicate the influence of each feature on predictions, making it a widely used baseline [7], [8]. XGBoost is a boosted tree algorithm that finds non-linear relationships and feature interactions in tabular data [9], [10]. Comparison of these models will evaluate if the additional flexibility of an ensemble learning approach makes it outperform a simple and understandable model in terms of detection performance.

However, current eye-tracking research shows significant differences in datasets, labeling methods, feature sets, and validation process, making it difficult to compare model families directly. Research comparing the performance of Logistic Regression and XGBoost used various eye-tracking setups and gave diverse results [11], [12], [13]. Furthermore, there were many studies where the models were tested on the same data used for training, thus overestimating the results for new users [14], [15]. Only a few studies described eye-tracking features used for each model, giving explanations for just one model [16], [17].

To address these gaps, the present study compares Logistic Regression and XGBoost for cognitive load detection using eye-tracking features derived from the publicly available COLET dataset [18]. The COLET dataset contains raw gaze, pupil, and blink data from 47 participants performing visual-search tasks under four conditions that vary time pressure and the presence of a secondary counting task. Both models are evaluated on participants excluded from training, and the study analyzes the eye-tracking features each model relies on using a consistent explanation framework (SHAP) for both models.
## PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION
This study develops and evaluates a machine learning framework for the detection of cognitive load from eye-tracking features. It directly compares Logistic Regression and XGBoost for the classification of low vs high cognitive load, using features that describe pupil size, blinks, fixations, saccades and gaze spread.

The framework involves a systematic workflow. Raw eye tracking data is acquired from the COLET dataset [18]. The single-task activity with no time pressure (A1) is designated as low load, and the dual-task activity with time pressure (A4) is designated as high load. The recordings are cleaned following published guidelines for Pupil Core data, fixations and saccades are detected with the velocity threshold and minimum fixation duration used by the COLET authors, and ten features are computed for each recording. Both models are then trained and evaluated with leave-one-participant-out validation, so that every prediction is made for a person whose labeled data were not used in training [14]. Each person's features are standardized using that person's recordings from all four activities, so their unlabeled recordings are used in that step.

In addition to comparing performance, the study analyzes feature importance to identify the eye-tracking indicators that each model relied on. Logistic Regression coefficients are reported, and SHAP values are computed for both models so that their rankings can be compared on the same scale [19], [20]. Permutation importance is computed as a model-agnostic check [21], [22].

The intended output is a comparative framework that shows how well each model distinguishes the low- and high-load conditions in participants whose labels were held out and which eye-tracking features drive their predictions. Because the counting task is spoken aloud, the study also tests a model that uses pupil features only, to check whether the results depend on effects of talking on the eyes [23].
## OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY
### General Objective
The general objective of this study is to compare Logistic Regression and XGBoost for cognitive load detection using eye-tracking features, and to analyze the features that each model relies on.
### Specific Objectives
Specifically, the study aims:

1.	To prepare whole-activity eye-tracking features (pupil, blink, fixation, saccade and gaze-dispersion measures) from the COLET dataset for binary classification of low (A1) versus high (A4) cognitive load.

2.	To train and evaluate Logistic Regression and XGBoost under leave-one-participant-out validation, with participant-grouped tuning and the same number of candidate hyperparameter settings for both models.

3.	To compare the performance of the two models using ROC-AUC, balanced accuracy, macro-F1, per-class recall and the Brier score, against a majority-class baseline.

4.	To determine whether the comparison holds when only pupil features are used, as a check against the effects of the spoken secondary task.

5.	To analyze and compare feature importance using Logistic Regression coefficients, SHAP values for both models and permutation importance, and to measure the agreement between the two models’ rankings.
## SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY
This study examines how well an interpretable model and an ensemble model can distinguish workload conditions from eye movements alone. Areas such as education, healthcare (where pupil size and blink rate have been used to assess workload in surgery [17], [25]), safety-critical work [3] and human–computer interaction could one day use this kind of monitoring, and they relate to Sustainable Development Goals 3, 4 and 9 [24]. Since this is a small laboratory study with a spoken task, it is only an early step and does not show that such tools would work in practice. The comparison between Logistic Regression and XGBoost also adds evidence, as in clinical prediction [26], on when interpretable models are sufficient.

For the research community, the study offers a fully specified evaluation on a public dataset, using participant-independent validation, with scaling and imputation fitted only on training data, practices that reduce overly optimistic results [15]; the per-person standardization, which uses each participant’s own unlabeled recordings, is stated as a limitation. Because COLET is openly available, other researchers can reproduce and extend the analysis.
## SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS
This study focuses on comparing Logistic Regression and XGBoost for cognitive load detection using eye-tracking features. It uses the publicly available COLET dataset [18], which contains raw Pupil Core recordings of 47 participants performing visual-search tasks in four activities. The analysis uses the two extreme activities: A1 (single task, no time pressure) as low load and A4 (counting backwards aloud under time pressure) as high load. After excluding recordings of insufficient quality and one duplicated set of recordings, 44 participants and 88 recordings are analyzed, one sample per whole activity.

The scope encompasses data preprocessing, fixation and saccade detection, extraction of ten eye-tracking features, participant-wise normalization, model training and tuning, leave-one-participant-out evaluation, and feature importance assessment. Two analyses are needed: the first one with all ten features, and the second one with only the two pupil features (mean and standard deviation of pupil diameter), which tests the effect of the spoken secondary task. In addition to the above, two pre-listed optional analyses are also conducted: the first one without blink rate and the second without participant-wise normalization. Further robustness analyses were added after the main results had been seen; they were not part of the pre-specified plan and are reported separately as post-hoc analyses (Chapter 4 and Appendix B).

The study has several limitations. It uses eye-tracking data only and does not include other signals such as electroencephalography or heart rate. It is limited to Logistic Regression and XGBoost and does not cover other machine learning or deep learning models. The data come from a laboratory task with a chin rest and a screen, so the findings may not transfer directly to real-world settings [27]. The sample of 44 participants is small, which widens the uncertainty of the results [28].

The high-load task involves speaking, which has been proven to increase the blink rate [23]. Talking and workload are not statistically separated in the experiment; rather, the authors provide a pupil-only model as an analysis robustness check. Even this model is not totally independent of talking, since the tracker recalculated the pupil model more often during the counting tasks. So the study detects COLET's task conditions, which mix dual-tasking, speaking and time pressure, and not cognitive load separated from speech. In post-hoc comparisons, time pressure was barely detectable when both activities involved speaking (A3 versus A4, ROC-AUC 0.60–0.66) and moderately detectable when neither did (A1 versus A2, 0.68–0.77), so the data cannot separate mental load from speech. Individual standardization relies on the recordings of each participant for all four tasks, including the tasks being classified, which makes the test much easier than meeting a total stranger: without it, ROC-AUC drops from 0.98–0.99 to 0.85–0.88 with all features and from 0.81–0.83 to 0.61–0.65 with pupil features only (Chapter 4). Subtracting each person’s A2 recording instead, which keeps A1 and A4 out of the reference, gave 0.90–0.92 with all features (post hoc).

Limitations of the study include the lack of real-time detection, eye-tracking hardware implementation, and testing on an external data set. Self-reported workload is used merely to validate differences between the groups, and not the classification task itself.
## CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK
The conceptual framework uses a sequential, multi-stage machine learning pipeline that transforms raw eye-tracking data into downstream classification performance and interpretability analyses (Figure 1).

The pipeline starts off with the extraction of gaze, pupil, and blink measurements from the COLET dataset. These measurements are then preprocessed to eliminate low confidence artifacts and determine the basic eye movement events including fixations and saccades [30], [31]. Task-based load labels are generated in the Experimental Configurations stage through identification of the extreme tasks; A1 as low load and A4 as high load tasks. The 10-dimensional Eye Tracking Feature set is then extracted from the processed measurements and normalized for each person to account for intrinsic variability among individuals in their eye movements.

These extracted features are simultaneously supplied to two types of models, namely the regularized linear model (Logistic Regression) and the non-linear ensemble model (XGBoost Model) [9]. Both models are trained and tested with a participant-disjoint Leave-One-Participant-Out (LOPO) Validation approach [33]. The cross-validated outputs are then funneled into twin analytical branches: Performance Evaluation, which tabulates discrimination metrics and the Brier score, and Feature Analysis, which uses SHAP and permutation frameworks to explain model behavior [22]. Ultimately, this framework yields three core deliverables: a comparative assessment of model performance, a ranking of the eye-tracking features each model relied on, checked with more than one importance measure, and tuned cognitive load classification models.

## OPERATIONAL DEFINITION OF TERMS
**Balanced Accuracy –** The average of the recall obtained for each class. In this study it is reported alongside ROC-AUC to summarize correct classification of both load levels.

**Binary Classification –** A task in which each observation is assigned to one of two classes. In this study, each recording is classified as low (A1) or high (A4) cognitive load.

**Blink Rate –** The number of blinks per minute of valid recording time. In this study it is one of the ten input features.

**Brier Score –** The mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes. In this study it summarizes the accuracy of the predicted probabilities; because it reflects both discrimination and calibration, a lower value alone does not show better calibration.

**Cognitive Load –** The mental effort required to perform a task. In this study it is operationalized by the COLET task condition: A1 as the low-load condition and A4 as the high-load condition. The models therefore classify workload conditions, which differ in more than mental effort (for example, A4 involves speaking), rather than a directly measured mental state.

**COLET Dataset –** A publicly available dataset of raw eye-tracking recordings from 47 participants performing visual-search tasks under four workload conditions. In this study it is the sole source of data.

**Elastic Net –** A penalty for regression models that combines L1 and L2 regularization. In this study it is used to keep Logistic Regression coefficients stable with a small sample.

**Eye Tracking –** The measurement of where and how the eyes move, and of pupil size, using a camera-based tracker. In this study the data were recorded with a Pupil Labs Pupil Core tracker.

**Feature Importance Analysis –** The analysis of how much each input feature contributes to a model’s predictions. In this study it uses Logistic Regression coefficients, SHAP values and permutation importance.

**Fixation –** A period in which the eyes remain relatively still on one location. In this study fixation rate and fixation duration are input features.

**F1-Score –** The harmonic mean of precision and recall. In this study the macro-averaged F1-score over both classes is reported.

**Gaze Dispersion –** The spread of gaze direction during a recording, measured as the standard deviation of gaze angle horizontally and vertically. In this study both directions are input features.

**I-VT (Velocity-Threshold Identification) –** An algorithm that labels eye samples as fixation or saccade depending on whether eye speed is below or above a threshold. In this study a threshold of 45°/s is used.

**Leave-One-Participant-Out (LOPO) Validation –** A validation procedure in which all data from one participant are held out for testing while the remaining participants are used for training, repeated for every participant.

**Logistic Regression –** A classification model that estimates the probability of a class from a weighted sum of input features. In this study it is the interpretable baseline model.

**NASA-RTLX –** The raw, unweighted version of the NASA Task Load Index questionnaire. In this study it is used only to confirm that the activities differed in workload.

**Per-Person Standardization –** Transforming each feature into a z-score using the mean and standard deviation of the same participant’s recordings. In this study it removes stable individual differences.

**Permutation Importance –** The drop in model performance when the values of one feature are randomly shuffled. In this study it is computed for both models on held-out predictions; because values are shuffled across participants, it shows how much a model relies on a feature under that shuffle, not the feature’s unique or causal contribution.

**Pupil Diameter –** The size of the pupil in millimetres, estimated by the tracker’s 3D eye model. In this study the mean and standard deviation of pupil diameter are input features.

**ROC-AUC –** The area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve, which measures how well a model ranks high-load above low-load recordings across all thresholds. In this study it is the primary metric.

**Saccade –** A rapid eye movement between fixations. In this study saccade rate, saccade amplitude and saccade peak velocity are input features.

**SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) –** A method that divides each prediction into the contribution of each feature. In this study it is applied to both models so their feature rankings can be compared.

**XGBoost –** An implementation of gradient-boosted decision trees that builds trees sequentially to correct earlier errors. In this study it is the ensemble model compared with Logistic Regression.

# CHAPTER 2 REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES
This chapter reviews the literature on cognitive load and its measurement, eye-tracking indicators of workload, the COLET dataset and its prior use, the use of Logistic Regression and XGBoost for workload classification, participant-independent validation, and feature importance analysis. It ends with a synthesis of the closest studies and the research gap addressed by this study.
## COGNITIVE LOAD AND ITS MEASUREMENT
Cognitive load describes the share of a person’s limited mental capacity that a task requires [1]. In cognitive load theory, working memory is limited, so tasks that exceed it impair learning and performance [2]. In ergonomics, mental workload is studied because of its relationship with performance and safety in complex work [3].

Workload is commonly measured in three ways: subjective ratings, performance measures and physiological signals. The NASA Task Load Index is the most widely used rating scale [34]; it asks participants to rate six dimensions of workload after a task [4], and its unweighted “raw” form is common in practice [34]. Ratings, however, are given after the task and reflect each person’s own judgement, and different workload measures are each sensitive to load but do not always agree [6]. Physiological measures are recorded continuously during the task. A systematic review of 91 studies found eye measures to be among the most widely used physiological indicators of workload [5].
## EYE-TRACKING INDICATORS OF COGNITIVE LOAD
Pupil diameter is the most established eye-tracking indicator of mental effort. The pupil dilates with increasing cognitive demand, but it also responds strongly to light, so luminance must be controlled or accounted for [35]. In the review by Tao et al., pupil diameter was significant in 79% of the studies that measured it [5].

The blink rate is equally sensitive to the level of work, although it is dependent on the type of task; mental work increases blink frequency while visual tasks decrease it [36]. The blink rate increases during speech [23], which is relevant to workload involving speech.

Saccades and fixations describe how the eyes move. Saccade amplitude has been reported to decrease under load [37], and saccadic peak velocity has been proposed as a workload index [38], [39]. Fixation rate and duration are related to both perceptual and cognitive load [40]. Under higher load, gaze also tends to concentrate in a smaller area, so measures of gaze dispersion can reflect workload [41], [42].

Because fixations and saccades are not measured directly, they must be detected from raw gaze samples. The velocity-threshold algorithm (I-VT) labels samples as saccades when eye speed exceeds a threshold [31]. Evaluations of detection algorithms show that results depend strongly on the chosen algorithm and thresholds, so settings should be reported and the output checked [43], [44].
## THE COLET DATASET AND ITS PRIOR USE
COLET was published by Ktistakis et al. in 2022 as an open dataset for cognitive workload estimation based on eye tracking [18]. Forty-seven participants solved visual-search puzzles in four activities that crossed two factors: time pressure and a secondary task of counting backwards aloud. Eye movements were recorded with a Pupil Labs Pupil Core tracker, and participants rated each activity with the NASA-RTLX. The authors extracted pupil, blink, fixation and saccade features and reported that Logistic Regression distinguished the single-task activity without time pressure (A1) from the multitask activity with time pressure (A4) with an accuracy of 0.85 (k-nearest neighbours reached 0.86). That result was obtained with a 20% hold-out test set and five-fold cross-validation that were not described as participant-independent, and with feature selection performed on the full dataset. An earlier conference paper by the same group described the approach [45].

Several later studies used COLET. Fuhl et al. proposed a feature based on the distribution of pupil diameters over time and evaluated it with a random split of 10–30 s windows [46]. In the work of Wibirama et al., deep learning was applied to eye movement metrics using overlapping windows at 80% and straightforward five-fold cross-validation [47], while Dell’Acqua et al. used large language models on symbolic gaze sequences with a 70/15/15 split of the 188 recordings, stratified by workload level [48]. Neither split was subject-based. These protocols allow data from the same participant, or even the same recording, to appear on both sides of the split. Fenoglio et al. applied federated learning to COLET and evaluated on unseen users through four-fold user-grouped cross-validation, using windowed features with Gaussian Naive Bayes, random forest and neural network models [49]. None of these studies applied Logistic Regression and XGBoost together, and none reported feature importance.
## LOGISTIC REGRESSION AND XGBOOST FOR COGNITIVE LOAD CLASSIFICATION
Logistic Regression models the probability of a class as a function of a weighted sum of features [7]. With small samples, its coefficients can become unstable, so regularization is used; the elastic net combines L1 and L2 penalties and handles groups of correlated features [50]. Kaczorowska et al. used elastic-net Logistic Regression for three-level workload classification from eye-tracking features and used its coefficients to rank feature importance [8].

XGBoost trains decision tree ensembles in a sequential manner with regularization for overfitting control [9]. Tree-based ensembles tend to work well with tabular data [10]. In workload studies, Walocha et al. optimized XGBoost using nested leave-one-participant-out validation and observed that shallow trees were mostly selected in their small dataset [51], whereas Shafiei et al. used XGBoost and SHAP along with EEG and eye tracking in a surgical task [17].

Studies that compared the two models directly reached different conclusions. Rolon-Merette et al. compared Logistic Regression, XGBoost and deep learning models on their own n-back data; when tested on held-out participants, XGBoost stayed above chance while Logistic Regression, which received raw time series, remained near chance [11]. Nerella et al. compared both models for cognitive load prediction in augmented reality [12], Chakraborty et al. compared Logistic Regression with boosting using eye-tracking data [52], and Shao et al. found no significant ROC-AUC difference between the two models with eye-only features in driving, although accuracy favored different models in different analyses [13]. More broadly, a systematic review in clinical prediction found no consistent performance benefit of machine learning over Logistic Regression [26]. A similar result for the two models therefore cannot be ruled out in advance.
## PARTICIPANT-INDEPENDENT VALIDATION AND DATA LEAKAGE
How the data set is split greatly influences the results. If records from the same subject are used in both training and test sets, the model identifies the subject rather than the condition, and an optimistic estimate of accuracy results; subject-independent validation better reflects real-world application to new subjects [14], [53]. Leaking also happens if preprocessing methods like feature selection or scaling are fit on the entire data set prior to splitting [15]. The hyperparameter tuning process must also be done within the training set, via nested cross-validation, to avoid optimistic results [33], [54]. Small sample sizes lead to large error bars for cross-validated estimates; thus, uncertainty must be reported [28].

Individual differences in eye behavior are large and stable [32], which is why many cross-participant workload studies standardize features within each participant [16], [56], [57], [58]. In an EEG workload study, z-score normalization gave the best cross-subject accuracy of the normalization schemes tested [59]. Preprocessing that uses test data is a recognized source of optimistic results [15]; because this step uses unlabeled data from the test participant, its effect on reported performance should be acknowledged.
## FEATURE IMPORTANCE ANALYSIS
Feature importance analysis identifies which inputs a model relies on. For linear models, coefficients on inputs placed on a common scale show the direction and relative size of each feature’s association with the outcome [60]. SHAP assigns each feature a share of every prediction based on Shapley values and can be applied to any model [19]; TreeSHAP computes these values efficiently for tree ensembles such as XGBoost [20]. Permutation importance measures the loss in performance when a feature is shuffled [21], [22]. Built-in importance measures of tree ensembles can be biased toward certain features, as shown for random forests [61], and importance should be read as what a model relied on, not as a causal effect [62].

In eye-tracking workload research, Božak et al. combined condition labels, leave-one-subject-out validation and SHAP explanations, and found subject-normalized features and fixation dispersion among the most important [16]. Xu et al., using wearable physiological sensors with nested leave-one-subject-out validation, cautioned that SHAP rankings computed from models trained on all data should be treated as exploratory [63]. These studies explained a single model or a single model family; Logistic Regression studies used coefficients [8], while tree-based studies used SHAP [17].

The studies that compared the two models directly disagree on whether XGBoost adds value over Logistic Regression [11], [13], and in clinical prediction machine learning has often brought no benefit over Logistic Regression [26]. Whether a boosted ensemble improves on a regularized linear model for small, tabular eye-tracking datasets under participant-independent evaluation therefore remains open. COLET offers a public setting for this question, but among the studies identified in the literature search of this study, none applied XGBoost or SHAP to COLET. On COLET, the one participant-independent evaluation found [49] used neither Logistic Regression, XGBoost nor feature importance, and the other COLET studies used splits that were not grouped by participant [18], [46], [47], [48]. This study addresses that gap by comparing the two models on COLET under leave-one-participant-out validation and by explaining both models with the same method.

# CHAPTER 3 METHODOLOGY
This chapter describes the research design, dataset, labels, preprocessing, feature extraction, models, validation procedure, evaluation metrics, feature importance analysis and ethical considerations of the study. Figure 2 gives an overview of the methodology.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 2.** Overview of the methodology.
## RESEARCH DESIGN
The study uses a quantitative, comparative design based on secondary analysis of a public dataset. Two classification models are trained and evaluated on the same features, with the same folds and the same number of candidate settings, so that differences in performance can be attributed to the models. To keep the analysis focused, only the steps needed for two pre-specified analyses are included: the main analysis (P1) with all ten features and a pupil-only analysis (P2). All thresholds and settings were fixed before any model was trained, after a data-quality inspection that summarized data by activity but did not compare feature values between A1 and A4, apart from the blink-presence and data-loss summaries by activity reported below.
## DATASET
The study uses COLET, version 3, downloaded from Zenodo (record 7766785) and released under a CC BY 4.0 license [18]. Table 2 summarizes the dataset.

**Table 2.** Description of the COLET dataset.

| **Item** | **Description** |
| undefined | undefined |
| Participants | 56 recruited; 9 excluded by the authors; 47 released (26 female, 21 male; age 32 ± 8 years) |
| Setting | Laboratory with chin and head rest; 24-inch screen (1280 × 720) at 80 cm; controlled lighting (400–450 lx) |
| Eye tracker | Pupil Labs Pupil Core, binocular; gaze ≈ 242 Hz, pupil ≈ 121 Hz per eye (measured; nominal 240 Hz); gaze resampled to a uniform 240 Hz grid |
| Task | Visual-search puzzles, five images per activity; activities in random order with 2-minute breaks |
| Design | 2 × 2: time pressure × secondary task (counting backwards aloud from 1000 in steps of 4) |
| Released data | Raw gaze, pupil and blink exports per participant and activity; NASA-RTLX per activity; no fixation or saccade events |
The dataset is distributed as a single 3.8 GB MATLAB file in which the recordings are nested: each of the 47 participants contains four activities, and each activity contains separate tables for gaze, pupil, blink and NASA-RTLX data. Because standard Python tools cannot read MATLAB table objects, the file was decoded once with the open-source mat-io package, after the archive’s checksum was verified, and flattened into one table per participant, activity and signal (Figure 3). This produced 564 Parquet files (188 recordings × 3 signals) and two CSV files holding the NASA-RTLX ratings and participant information. Parquet is an open, compressed file format for tables that stores the same rows and columns as a CSV file but loads much faster for large data. No values were changed; cells containing non-numeric objects were stored as text. The flattened gaze files contain about 2.25 million samples and the pupil files about 4.51 million samples, from which the preprocessing described below produces one row of ten features for each of the 88 analyzed recordings.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 3.** Structure of the COLET data before and after flattening.
## LABELS AND UNIT OF ANALYSIS
Labels are taken from the experimental conditions. For every participant, activity A1 (single task, no time pressure) is labeled low load and activity A4 (counting aloud under time pressure) is labeled high load. The visual search task is constant for all activities. The high load is achieved through the addition of another concurrent verbal task of counting backward by fours. It is a dual-task experiment since the high-load condition differs from the low-load condition in speech due to the nature of the additional task being verbal. The middle conditions, A2 and A3, are left out of the classification, following studies that compare the extremes of a workload manipulation [25], [64]. Condition labels are used rather than self-reports because ratings are affected by how each participant uses the rating scale [34].

The NASA-RTLX ratings collected by the COLET authors [18], the common unweighted form of the NASA-TLX [34], are used as a manipulation check. A Friedman test compares the ratings across the four activities, and each participant’s A4 rating is compared with their A1 rating. In the released data, all 47 participants rated A4 higher than A1.

Because the activities are short (11 to 141 s), the unit of analysis is one sample per whole activity, the same unit used by the COLET authors [18]. This gives two samples per participant (Table 3).

## DATA PREPROCESSING
COLET provides raw tracker data, so the signals must be cleaned before features can be computed. The preprocessing has four stages (Figure 4): removing bad data, cleaning each signal, detecting fixations and saccades, and computing features. Table 4 lists each step and its source.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 4.** Preprocessing stages.

**Table 4.** Preprocessing steps.

| **Step** | **Procedure** | **Source** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined |
| Time alignment | Pupil and blink data trimmed to each recording’s gaze time range (stray samples found in one participant) | Data check |
| Sample validity | Samples with tracker confidence below 0.8 treated as invalid | [30], [65] |
| Recording exclusion | Recordings with more than 35% invalid samples excluded; participants missing A1 or A4 dropped (P06, P17); duplicated recordings kept once (P31 dropped) | [66] |
| Valid time | Blink rate computed over valid recording time (gaps longer than 1 s excluded); fixation and saccade rates over time with a valid gaze direction | Data check |
| Blinks | Tracker blink events merged if less than 100 ms apart, then kept if 50–500 ms (own choice around the typical ~200 ms blink); blink periods treated as missing | [67], [68] |
| Gaze gaps | Gaps shorter than 75 ms linearly interpolated; longer gaps left missing | [30] |
| Pupil | 3D-model diameter in mm; 1.5–9 mm range; dilation-speed outlier removal (median + 16 MAD, the default of the authors’ published code); both eyes averaged; gaps up to 250 ms filled; 4 Hz low-pass filter; model refits counted | [29], [68], [69] |
| Gaze direction | Each eye’s unit gaze direction vector, averaged across the two eyes and resampled to a uniform 240 Hz grid; velocity from the change in direction (see Fixation and Saccade Detection) | [70], [71], [72] |
| Quality report | Share of valid samples reported per recording and condition; never used as a feature | [30] |
Recording exclusion removed three of 188 recordings (P06 A3, P06 A4 and P17 A4). Because P06 and P17 lack a valid A1–A4 pair, they are dropped. In addition, the released gaze, pupil and blink files of P28 and P31 are byte-identical in all four activities, although the two participants’ demographic data and NASA-RTLX ratings differ; one person’s eye recordings are therefore stored twice, and their owner cannot be determined. The recordings are kept once (as P28), and both IDs are left out of the NASA-RTLX analyses. This leaves 44 participants and 88 balanced samples.

Gaze angles are computed from each eye’s own gaze direction rather than from the tracker’s combined 3D gaze point. The 3D gaze point depends on an estimate of viewing distance from the angle between the two eyes, and pupil-based video eye trackers do not measure vergence accurately enough to determine the viewing distance, as shown at 77 cm with a desktop tracker [70]; with Pupil Core, gaze depth was severely underestimated [71]. In COLET this estimate was implausible: the median estimated distance was about 113 mm against a true viewing distance of 800 mm, and some samples were placed behind the camera. Eye speed is therefore computed from the change in direction of the gaze vector, averaged across the two eyes, following the vector-angle approach used for Pupil Labs data by Kothari et al. [72]. Samples with only one valid eye are treated as missing and handled by the gap rule, because each eye’s direction alone was biased inward by about 10° in these data; this follows the practice of treating unreliable samples as gaps [30].
## FIXATION AND SACCADE DETECTION
Fixations and saccades are detected with the velocity-threshold algorithm (I-VT) [31], using the velocity threshold and minimum fixation duration of the COLET authors [18]. The gaze directions are first resampled to a uniform 240 Hz grid, and eye velocity is computed with a five-point smoothed central difference of the unit gaze vectors; velocity filtering of this kind is described by Duchowski [73], but the coefficients used here are the researchers’ own choice. Velocities above 1000°/s are rejected as artifacts [74]. Samples faster than 45°/s are classified as saccades, and fixations shorter than 55 ms are discarded; both values follow COLET [18]. The 45°/s threshold corresponds to the minimum peak velocity of human-coded saccades in Andersson et al., and the 55 ms minimum to the human-derived minimum fixation duration in the same study [43]. Neither value was validated for a 240 Hz Pupil Core; the 55 ms minimum lies within the 50–75 ms range evaluated by Trabulsi et al. [75].

Because detection results depend on the algorithm and its settings [43], [44], a sanity check is applied to each activity separately before the features are used: the median fixation duration must lie between 150 and 400 ms, and the ratio of saccades to fixations must lie between 0.8 and 1.25. If either condition fails in any activity, the main analysis uses only the five features that do not depend on event detection (pupil mean, pupil standard deviation, blink rate and gaze dispersion in both directions), following the use of feature subsets in prior work [16]. The tolerance of 0.8–1.25 is the researchers’ own choice.
## FEATURE EXTRACTION
Ten features are computed for each whole activity (Table 5). Blink rate is expressed per minute of valid recording time. Fixation and saccade rates are expressed per second of time with a valid gaze direction, because gaze is missing more often in the high-load activity and events cannot be detected while it is missing. The feature set is fixed in advance and is the same in every fold, which keeps feature importance comparable across folds.

**Table 5.** Eye-tracking features.

| **Group** | **Feature** | **Support** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined |
| Pupil | Pupil diameter mean; pupil diameter standard deviation | [5], [18], [35] |
| Blink | Blink rate (per minute) | [5], [36] |
| Fixation | Fixation rate; mean fixation duration | [5], [40] |
| Saccade | Saccade rate; mean saccade amplitude; mean saccade peak velocity | [5], [37], [38] |
| Gaze dispersion | Standard deviation of gaze angle, horizontal and vertical | [16], [41] |
Some features used in prior work are excluded. Blink duration is undefined when no blink occurs, which happened only in low-load recordings (13 of 44 A1 recordings and none of the A4 recordings); its missingness would therefore reveal the label [15]. Mean saccade velocity and saccade duration are near-duplicates of peak velocity and amplitude (ρ = 0.95 and 0.83 in a preliminary data inspection; 0.99 and 0.80 in the final features) [16], [76]. The higher-order statistics used by the COLET authors are omitted to keep the number of features small relative to the 88 samples. Because pupil size also responds to light [35], stimulus brightness was considered: room lighting was controlled at 400–450 lx, and although the puzzle images differ in brightness, the COLET authors found pupil size following image brightness in only 2 of 47 participants [18]. No further luminance correction is applied, which is stated as a limitation.
## PER-PERSON STANDARDIZATION
Each feature is converted to a z-score using the mean and standard deviation of the same participant’s four activities. This removes stable individual differences, in eye movements [32] and pupil size [11], which are much larger than the workload effect, and follows the closest prior studies [16], [56], [57]. The step does not use labels. It does, however, use the test participant’s own unlabeled recordings and relies on COLET’s balanced design, in which every participant completed both easier and harder activities; this is stated as a limitation.
## MODEL DEVELOPMENT
Training is done on two models (Table 6). Logistic Regression employs an elastic-net penalty where the penalty weight and L1/L2 ratio are optimized within the training folds [8], [50]. Shallow regularized trees are used in XGBoost as only 86 samples (43 subjects) can be trained in each fold [9], [51]. The two models are presented with the same number of parameter candidates (by design, as their parameter spaces differ in size, this does not mean the same level of tuning) and the same folds, and tuning is nested to avoid selection bias [33]. Imputation for Logistic Regression uses the median value from the training fold while missingness is natively supported by XGBoost; native handling was shown to be comparable to median imputation for gradient boosting [77]. Median imputation without missingness indicators is a simplification; it was never used as there were no missing values in any of the features.

**Table 6.** Model settings.

| **Model** | **Settings searched** |
| undefined | undefined |
| Logistic Regression | Elastic-net penalty; C log-uniform 10⁻³–10²; L1 ratio 0–1; features standardized in-fold |
| XGBoost | Maximum depth 1–3; 50–300 trees; learning rate 0.05–0.1; row and column subsampling 0.7–1.0; L2 penalty 0.01–10 and L1 penalty 0.001–1 (log-uniform) |
## VALIDATION PROCEDURE
Models are evaluated with leave-one-participant-out validation over the 44 participants: in each fold, both recordings of one participant form the test set and the other 43 participants form the training set [14], [53]. Hyperparameters are tuned by random search with 30 candidate settings per model, scored by ROC-AUC in a five-fold inner cross-validation that is also grouped by participant [33], [54]. The in-fold scaling and imputation are fitted on the training participants only [15]. Per-person standardization is the one exception: it uses each participant’s own unlabeled recordings, including those of the test participant (see Per-Person Standardization).
## PERFORMANCE METRICS AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS
The primary metric is ROC-AUC computed on the pooled out-of-fold predictions [78], with a 95% confidence interval from a bootstrap that resamples participants (2000 resamples) [28]. Balanced accuracy, macro-F1, per-class recall and the Brier score [79], [80] are also reported, together with a majority-class baseline [16] and the share of participants whose A4 recording is ranked above their A1 recording.

The two models are compared through the difference in pooled ROC-AUC with a participant-bootstrap confidence interval. A paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test on each participant’s margin, the predicted probability for A4 minus that for A1, is reported as a supporting test; because margins depend on each model’s probability scale, it is secondary to the ROC-AUC difference. The test is adapted from comparisons across datasets to comparisons across participants [81], and a grouped permutation test, in which each participant’s two labels are swapped at random, checks performance against chance [82]. The permutation test uses default parameters of each model, hence making the actual run and the permutation equivalent, implying that the calculated p-value refers to the untuned pipeline, while the headline number is the nested ROC-AUC for the tuned model; the lowest possible p-value using 200 permutations equals 1/201 ≈ 0.005.
## FEATURE IMPORTANCE ANALYSIS
Feature importance is analyzed in three ways. First, the standardized elastic-net coefficients of Logistic Regression are reported [8]. Second, SHAP values are computed on held-out data for both models, using TreeSHAP for XGBoost and linear SHAP for Logistic Regression, so that both rankings are on the same scale [19], [20]. It is the choice of the authors to utilize SHAP on both the models as SHAP is applicable to all models. The linear explainer adopts the interventional approach where the features are taken as independent variables; however, since there are a few eye features that are interdependent, the attribution reflects the reliance on the model. TreeSHAP is run without background data and therefore uses the tree-path-dependent convention, which follows the dependencies between features in the training data, so the two rankings rest on slightly different assumptions about correlated features. Third, permutation importance is computed for both models on the pooled out-of-fold predictions, with 50 repeats per feature [21], [22].

Agreement between the two models’ rankings is measured with Kendall’s τ, reported with a bootstrap confidence interval, and the stability of the model weights across folds is examined, in the spirit of feature-selection stability analysis [83]. Built-in gain importance is reported in the appendix only, because built-in importance can be biased, as shown for random forests [61]. Importance is interpreted as what each model relied on, not as a cause of cognitive load [62].
## ANALYSIS PLAN
Two analyses are required (Table 7). The main analysis (P1) uses all ten features. Because the high-load activity involves counting aloud, which raises the blink rate [23], [84], a second analysis (P2) repeats P1 with the two pupil features only, since pupil size is the most established workload signal [5] and has been used alone in prior workload models [11], [85], [86].

**Table 7.** Required analyses.

| **Analysis** | **Features** | **Purpose** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined |
| P1 | All 10 features | Main comparison of Logistic Regression and XGBoost |
| P2 | Pupil mean and pupil standard deviation | Robustness check against effects of talking |
P1 is the headline result regardless of which analysis scores higher. A ceiling rule was stated before any results were seen: if both models exceed 0.95 ROC-AUC in P1, the model comparison is interpreted mainly from P2, because top-performing models often tie [8], while feature importance is still reported from P1. Analyses added after the results had been seen are reported separately as post-hoc analyses (Chapter 4 and Appendix B) and do not change the pre-specified ones. P2 is not fully independent of the spoken task, because the tracker re-fitted its pupil model more often in the counting activities; this is stated as a limitation.
## IMPLEMENTATION
The pipeline was implemented in Python 3.11 with NumPy 2.2.4, pandas 2.3.1, SciPy 1.15.2, scikit-learn 1.7.1, XGBoost 3.2.0 and SHAP 0.51.0, and every threshold is held in a single configuration file. All random processes use a fixed seed, so repeated runs in the same environment and package versions give identical results. A Google Colab notebook with the same pinned package versions allows the analysis to be reproduced. The pipeline was tested on synthetic data with a known structure before it was applied to COLET. The full analysis was run once after all settings had been fixed, and repeated once, with no change to any setting, after two participant IDs were found to hold the same recordings. A shuffled-label control and the robustness analyses in Chapter 4 and Appendix B were added after that as post-hoc checks.
## ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS
This study is a secondary analysis of the publicly available, de-identified COLET dataset (CC BY 4.0), whose collection was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Foundation for Research and Technology – Hellas (110/12-02-2021) [18]. No new data were collected, and no attempt is made to identify participants. The dataset and the original article are cited as required by the license.
## DESIGN CHOICES
Some settings have no published source for their exact value and are the researchers’ own choices, justified by the data checks described above: the 35% exclusion threshold applied to whole recordings, the 1 s gap rule for valid time, the 0.8–1.25 tolerance of the detection sanity check, the use of each eye’s gaze direction, treating samples with only one valid eye as missing, merging blinks before applying the 50–500 ms range, a 120 Hz grid and a second-order Butterworth filter for the pupil signal, the 240 Hz resampling grid, and the five-point velocity filter.

One limitation of the event detection is also noted here. A blink or a gap longer than 75 ms inside a fixation splits it into two, and blinks were far more frequent in the high-load activity. This would tend to raise the fixation rate and shorten fixations in A4; the gaze-time denominator corrects the rates for missing time but not for this splitting.

# CHAPTER 4 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
This chapter presents the results in the order of the analysis: the manipulation check, data quality, the event-detection sanity check, the features, the two required analyses, the model comparison, feature importance, and a shuffled-label check. It ends with a discussion of the findings against the related studies in Chapter 2. All values come from a run made after every setting had been fixed. The run was repeated once, with no change to any setting, after two participant IDs were found to hold the same recordings (Chapter 3). The shuffled-label check was added after that as a post-hoc check.
## MANIPULATION CHECK
The NASA-RTLX ratings increased for all four activities (Table 8, Figure 5). The significance of differences in the rated workload among the activities was tested by means of Friedman’s test and found to be significant (χ²(3) = 82.72, p < 0.001, n = 43; P28 and P31 are not included as the owner of the recordings they share is unknown). All 43 participants rated A4 higher than A1, with a median difference of 31.7 points. Thus, NASA-RTLX ratings showed that the workload reported for A4 was higher than that for A1; the labels reflect a validated difference in subjective workload between these task conditions, although the conditions also differ in speaking and time pressure.

## DATA QUALITY AND RETENTION
Of the 188 recordings, three exceeded the 35% invalid-sample limit and were excluded: P06 A3 (57.4% invalid), P06 A4 (38.8%) and P17 A4 (48.6%). Participants P06 and P17 therefore lacked a valid A1–A4 pair and were dropped. In addition, P31 was dropped because its recordings are identical to those of P28 (Chapter 3). This left 44 participants, each with all four activities retained, and 88 samples for the classification. Table 9 summarizes data quality per activity.

**Table 9.** Data quality per activity (retained recordings).

| **Activity** | **Invalid samples (median)** | **Samples with both eyes (median)** | **Recordings with a pupil-model refit** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined | undefined |
| A1 | 0.9% | 99.5% | 8 |
| A2 | 0.7% | 99.5% | 11 |
| A3 | 6.9% | 98.6% | 20 |
| A4 | 6.9% | 98.7% | 18 |
Invalid samples were about eight times more frequent in the counting activities, consistent with more blinking and with tracking loss while talking; outside blink periods, data loss was also several times higher in A3 and A4. The requirement that both eyes be valid removed little data (about 1% of samples). Pupil-model refits were about twice as common in the counting activities (38 vs 19 recordings), which is the reason P2 is not fully independent of the spoken task. None of the ten features had missing values in any activity, so imputation played no role in the results.
## EVENT-DETECTION SANITY CHECK
The sanity check performed beforehand has proven successful for all activities (Table 10). Median fixation times lie between 212.5 and 235.4 ms, and within the 150-400 ms interval, while the ratio of saccades to fixations is between 0.93 and 0.99, within the 0.8-1.25 interval. Thus, the events detected are reasonable, and P1 utilized all ten features as expected instead of the five-feature backup plan.

## MAIN ANALYSIS (P1)
With all ten features, both models separated low from high load almost perfectly in participants whose labels were held out from training (Table 12, Figures 6 and 7). Logistic Regression reached a pooled ROC-AUC of 0.992 (95% CI 0.979–1.000) and XGBoost 0.980 (0.957–0.997). The majority-class baseline reached a balanced accuracy of 0.500, against 0.966 and 0.920 for the two models. Both models ranked the A4 recording above the A1 recording for all 44 participants. The Grouped Permutation Test, performed with default settings, resulted in the untuned pipeline being superior to chance level (ROC-AUC 0.991 on the Logistic Regression model and 0.977 on the XGBoost; p-value 0.005, the smallest possible).

**Figure 7.** Pooled ROC-AUC with 95% participant-bootstrap confidence intervals.

In both cases, the ROC-AUC score was above 0.95 for P1, so the pre-stated ceiling principle was used: the two classifiers cannot be distinguished in P1 and the analysis is primarily done using the results from P2. The chosen settings for Logistic Regression were different in different folds (median C = 4.97, IQR 65.3; median L1 ratio 0.69), while XGBoost mostly chose depth 2 (20 out of 44, and depth 1 in 16; median 192 trees). In P2, depth 1 was mostly chosen by XGBoost (37 out of 44) and a stronger penalty by Logistic Regression (median C = 0.15).
## PUPIL-ONLY ANALYSIS (P2)
With only the mean and standard deviation of pupil diameter, both models remained well above chance (Table 12). Logistic Regression reached 0.831 (0.735–0.912) and XGBoost 0.812 (0.697–0.912); both permutation tests gave p = 0.005 (untuned ROC-AUC 0.852 and 0.819). Because blinking, the feature most directly raised by speaking [23], is left out, this result indicates that the discrimination does not depend solely on blink-rate input; speech-related effects on the pupil, pupil-model refits and other condition differences cannot be ruled out. The drop from P1 to P2 (about 0.16–0.17 in ROC-AUC) indicates how much the non-pupil features, above all the blink rate, added.
## MODEL COMPARISON
Table 13 compares the two models.

**Table 13.** Comparison of XGBoost with Logistic Regression.

| **Analysis** | **AUC difference, XGBoost − LR (95% CI)** | **Wilcoxon on per-participant margins** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined |
| P1 | −0.012 (−0.030 to 0.002) | p = 0.112 |
| P2 | −0.019 (−0.086 to 0.047) | p = 0.007, larger margins for XGBoost |
In P1 the two models were practically identical, as the ceiling rule anticipated. In P2, which the rule designates for the comparison, XGBoost scored 0.019 lower than Logistic Regression. The confidence interval of this difference includes zero, so the pooled ROC-AUC does not establish a difference. The per-participant margins, the gap between each person’s predicted probabilities for A4 and A1, were larger for XGBoost in 29 of the 44 participants (Wilcoxon p = 0.007), so the two metrics point in different directions; pooled ROC-AUC, the pre-specified primary metric, was kept as the main comparison. This partly reflects the more extreme probabilities of XGBoost: Logistic Regression was strongly regularized in P2 (median C = 0.15), which pulls its probabilities towards 0.5, and margins depend on each model’s probability scale. The margins therefore describe how confident each model was, not how well it separated the two conditions. Overall, there was no evidence that XGBoost performed better. In the pre-specified comparison no difference could be detected at this sample size, and across the secondary and post-hoc analyses Logistic Regression scored equal or higher in most settings, significantly so without blink rate (below), with 10 s windows (Appendix B) and with unstandardized pupil features for A1 versus A2. No equivalence margin was set in advance, so the results do not show that the two models are equal either. Tuning also added no benefit at n = 88: in P2 the untuned models scored 0.852 (Logistic Regression) and 0.819 (XGBoost), against 0.831 and 0.812 after tuning. P2 is, however, a low-dimensional test: mean pupil diameter carried almost all the information, and XGBoost chose single-split trees in 37 of 44 folds, so this comparison cannot test its ability to model interactions between features.

The omission of individual standardization (a pre-specified optional analysis using nested tuning) led to an AUC of 0.853 for the logistic regression model and 0.881 for the XGBoost model in P1 and 0.611 and 0.649 in P2. For differences in XGBoost – Logistic Regression, this gave results of +0.028 (−0.034 to +0.094) in P1 and +0.038 (−0.060 to +0.129) in P2. The confidence intervals contain zero in both cases, while point estimations favor XGBoost without standardization and Logistic Regression with it, which means that the models' ranking depends on the evaluation procedure used. Removing blink rate in P1 (another pre-listed optional analysis) brought the ROC-AUC to 0.929 for Logistic Regression and 0.886 for XGBoost, resulting in −0.043 (−0.084 to −0.007) difference, which is the only pre-specified comparison with an interval not containing zero.
## FEATURE IMPORTANCE
By SHAP value, both models relied on the same three features most (Figure 8): blink rate, mean pupil diameter and fixation rate. The rankings of the two models agreed (Kendall’s τ = 0.69, 95% CI 0.60–0.73, computed on each feature’s mean absolute SHAP value). Permutation importance agreed on blink rate: shuffling it lowered the pooled ROC-AUC by 0.30 for Logistic Regression and 0.27 for XGBoost. Mean pupil diameter mattered much less to XGBoost, with a drop of 0.04 against 0.12 for Logistic Regression, and XGBoost’s gain importance ranked saccade rate second (Appendix A). The agreement between the models is therefore clearest for blink rate. Because the values are shuffled across participants, these drops show how much each model relies on a feature under that shuffle, not a feature’s unique contribution, and the SHAP rankings are descriptive because the two explainers make different assumptions about feature dependence.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 8.** Mean absolute SHAP value per feature in P1 for both models.

The Logistic Regression coefficients show the direction of each effect (Table 14). A higher blink rate and a larger pupil pushed predictions towards high load, while a higher fixation rate and a wider gaze spread pushed them towards low load; these five coefficients kept the same sign in at least 89% of the folds. Because fixation and saccade rates are strongly related and blink rate is in the model, these signs are conditional on the other features and should not be read as single-feature directions. The elastic-net penalty set the remaining saccade and pupil-variability coefficients to zero in many folds. Gain importance for XGBoost is reported in Appendix A (Table A1).

## SHUFFLED-LABEL CHECK
Because near-perfect results can signal leakage, the pipeline was rerun with default hyperparameters and shuffled labels after the main analysis, as a post-hoc check that was not part of the pre-specified plan. The average ROC-AUC over 40 runs dropped to 0.49 and 0.53 respectively for the Logistic Regression and XGBoost classifiers when label assignments were randomized between subjects; with label shuffling performed over all recordings, the average ROC-AUC fell to 0.46 and 0.53 respectively. The unoptimized pipeline thus does well only with true labels. This negative control tests only whether the procedure learns from the labels by chance; it cannot detect other problems, such as duplicated recordings or the use of each test participant’s unlabeled recordings in standardization, which are discussed below. The individual features explain why the problem is easy. For example, blink rate alone distinguished A1 from A4 with a ROC-AUC of 0.89 on raw values and 0.97 after per-person standardization, and 42 out of 44 participants blinked more in A4. So the full ten-feature models added only about 0.01 to 0.02 over standardized blink rate alone (0.992 and 0.980).
## POST-HOC ROBUSTNESS ANALYSES
The analyses in this section were added after the main results had been seen, in response to the questions above about standardization, speech and the strength of single features. They were not part of the pre-specified plan and should be read as exploratory. They used the same nested leave-one-participant-out procedure, seed and participant bootstrap as the main analysis, and no correction for multiple comparisons was applied across them.

First, per-person standardization was replaced with A2-baseline centering: each participant’s A2 values were subtracted from their A1 and A4 values, so the two classified recordings played no part in the reference. A single recording has no standard deviation, so the values were centered but not divided; Logistic Regression rescaled them within each training fold, and XGBoost does not depend on scale. All 44 participants had a valid A2 recording. ROC-AUC fell from 0.992 to 0.903 for Logistic Regression and from 0.980 to 0.921 for XGBoost (Table 15). These values are comparable to or modestly above those without any standardization (0.853 and 0.881), which lie inside their confidence intervals. Part of the main result therefore comes from standardizing over the test participant’s own A1 and A4, but the separation stays strong when a third recording is the only reference. A2 is itself a time-pressure activity and not a neutral rest recording.

Second, simpler models were run as baselines. Logistic Regression trained on blink rate alone reached 0.963 with standardized values and 0.883 without; these differ slightly from the single-feature values in the previous section, which ranked the feature values directly without a model. Blink rate and mean pupil diameter together reached 0.973 (Logistic Regression) and 0.970 (XGBoost), close to but below the ten-feature models. Default hyperparameters gave 0.991 and 0.977 in P1, so tuning added nothing at n = 88. Blink rate alone therefore carries nearly all of the P1 result.

Third, two other pairs of activities were classified to separate speaking from time pressure (Table 16). A3 and A4 both involve counting aloud and differ only in time pressure; A1 and A2 are both silent and also differ only in time pressure. With standardized features, A3 versus A4 reached ROC-AUC 0.60–0.66, and only the pupil-only XGBoost model had a confidence interval above 0.5; without standardization the models were at chance level (0.44–0.53). A1 versus A2 reached 0.68–0.77 with standardized features and 0.50–0.64 without. Time pressure was therefore hard to detect while participants were speaking and moderately detectable while they were silent. Both contrasts vary time pressure only, which the COLET authors found to be a weak manipulation [18], so they show that time pressure is hard to detect during speech, not that mental effort cannot be detected. With 44 pairs, the confidence intervals are wide. Compared with A1 versus A4 (0.98–0.99), these results indicate that most of the main separation comes from the speaking component of A4.

## DISCUSSION
The near-perfect separation in P1 reflects two properties of the evaluation design, and both limit what the result shows. First, the high-load activity added a spoken secondary task, and speaking raises the blink rate [23]; blink rate was the strongest feature for both models. The eye measures in this study therefore capture the dual-task condition as a whole, including its speech component, and not mental effort alone. Second, per-person standardization removes stable differences between people [32]. This helped most for pupil size, whose single-feature ROC-AUC rose from 0.62 to 0.87, but it uses each test participant’s own unlabeled recordings, including the two being classified, and so makes the test easier than meeting a complete stranger. Without per-person standardization, ROC-AUC fell to 0.853–0.881 in P1 and 0.611–0.649 in P2, so much of the reported performance depends on this calibration, especially for pupil size. The pupil-only result (ROC-AUC 0.81–0.83) indicates that discrimination does not depend solely on the most speech-sensitive feature, although pupil-model refits and any pupil response to speaking cannot be excluded; this is in line with the strong support for pupil size as a workload measure [5], [35].

The post-hoc analyses make both points more concrete. When the reference was a separate activity (A2) rather than all four, ROC-AUC was still 0.90–0.92, close to the 0.85–0.88 without standardization, so the calibration effect is real but does not explain the whole result. When speaking was held constant (A3 versus A4), time pressure was detected only weakly (0.60–0.66), and blink rate alone reached 0.963. The models therefore detect COLET’s task condition, which includes speaking, and these data cannot separate mental load from speech.

The COLET authors reported an accuracy of 0.85 for Logistic Regression on the same A1-versus-A4 task with a split that was not described as participant-independent [18]. Here, Logistic Regression reached a balanced accuracy of 0.966 (equal to accuracy, because the classes are balanced) under a participant-independent protocol: no labeled data from the test participant were used, but their unlabeled recordings were used for standardization, and without that step balanced accuracy was 0.739 (Table 12). The higher value is therefore not explained by labeled participant overlap. Plausible reasons are the per-person standardization, which uses each test participant’s own unlabeled recordings, and the whole-activity features, which average out moment-to-moment noise; the unstandardized analysis supports the first reason, since ROC-AUC without standardization was 0.853 for Logistic Regression in P1. The two results are not directly comparable because the protocols differ.

XGBoost did not clearly outperform Logistic Regression. This is in line with Shao et al., who found no significant ROC-AUC difference between the two models with eye-only features [13], and with the finding that machine-learning models often bring no benefit over Logistic Regression in clinical prediction [26]. It differs from Rolon-Merette et al., where XGBoost clearly beat Logistic Regression [11]; there, however, Logistic Regression received raw time series, whereas here both models received the same ten summary features. With 88 samples and one dominant feature, the extra flexibility of boosted trees has little to exploit. Without per-person standardization, however, XGBoost’s point estimates were higher than those of Logistic Regression, although not significantly, so this conclusion holds for the calibrated protocol and should not be generalized beyond it.

Longer fixations under high load agree with the pattern reported in the workload literature [5], whereas the COLET authors reported shorter fixations [18]. Other directions differed from the literature: saccades became slightly larger and faster, unlike the decreases reported earlier [37], [38], and gaze spread increased rather than concentrated [41], [42]. Saccade rate fell, whereas the COLET authors reported an increase. These differences may come from the different gaze-to-angle conversion and event detection, and from speaking during A4. For the time-pressure contrast (A1 versus A2), the direction of change matched what the COLET authors reported for every feature. Under multitasking, however, the saccade rate and velocity changed little here, whereas the COLET authors reported a doubling. Their reported A1 saccade and fixation rates (1.71 and 2.50 per second) and median saccade amplitude (14°) also differ from the values found here. The cause was not tested; it may lie in the different gaze-to-angle conversion or event-detection settings. Blinking and gaps during tracking may cause segmenting of fixations, and since segments shorter than 55 ms are disregarded, this could increase or decrease the number of fixations. These factors’ influence on the difference between A1 and A4 was not measured. The resulting features showed that the mean speed of saccades and saccade duration, which were disregarded before, were almost identical to peak speed and amplitude (Chapter 3).

# CHAPTER 5 CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION
## SUMMARY OF FINDINGS
This study compared Logistic Regression and XGBoost for detecting cognitive load from eye-tracking features on the COLET dataset, using leave-one-participant-out validation and feature importance analysis for both models. The main findings are the following.

1.	Ten whole-activity features (pupil, blink, fixation, saccade and gaze-spread measures) were prepared for 44 participants, after one duplicated set of recordings in the released data was removed. The event-detection sanity check passed in all four activities, and no feature had missing values.

2.	Under leave-one-participant-out validation, both models distinguished the low-load activity (A1) from the high-load activity (A4) almost perfectly (ROC-AUC 0.992 for Logistic Regression and 0.980 for XGBoost; balanced accuracy 0.966 and 0.920; Brier score 0.032 and 0.060; majority-class baseline 0.500).

3.	Since both the models had surpassed the predetermined ceiling value of 0.95, the comparison was drawn from the pupil-only analysis where the scores were Logistic Regression 0.831, XGBoost 0.812. The statistical comparison of the pooled ROC-AUC showed no detectable difference at this sample size. Neither model proved superior consistently, and there was no evidence that XGBoost performed better. Without individual standardization ROC-AUC dropped to 0.853-0.881 in P1 and 0.611-0.649 in P2.

4.	With pupil features alone, both models remained well above chance, consistent with a load-related pupil signal beyond the most obvious effects of speaking, although pupil-model refits and any pupil response to speaking itself cannot be excluded.

5.	Both models relied mainly on blink rate, mean pupil diameter and fixation rate, and their SHAP feature rankings agreed (Kendall’s τ = 0.69; same three leading features). Permutation importance confirmed blink rate as the leading feature for both models, while mean pupil diameter mattered much less to XGBoost than to Logistic Regression, and the Logistic Regression coefficients kept stable signs for the five leading features.

6.	In post-hoc analyses that were not part of the pre-specified plan, subtracting each participant’s A2 recording instead of standardizing over all four activities gave ROC-AUC 0.90–0.92 in P1. Blink rate alone gave 0.963, and default hyperparameters matched the tuned models. With speaking held constant (A3 versus A4), time pressure was detected only weakly (0.60–0.66); between the two silent activities (A1 versus A2) it reached 0.68–0.77.
## CONCLUSIONS
Eye-tracking features can detect a high-load dual-task condition in people whose labels were held out from training, and XGBoost did not outperform a simple, interpretable Logistic Regression (the upper 95% bound of the ROC-AUC difference was 0.002 in P1 and 0.047 in P2). The ranking of the two models depends on the evaluation protocol: without per-person standardization, XGBoost’s point estimates were higher, although not significantly. No difference between the two models could be detected with this feature set and sample size; since no equivalence margin was set, this does not show that they perform equally. The two models also agreed, by SHAP value, on which eye measures mattered most, especially blink rate.

The results must be read with the design of COLET in mind. The high-load activity added a spoken arithmetic task, and the strongest feature, blink rate, is also raised by speaking. The study therefore shows that eye features detect a dual-task condition that includes speech; the pupil-only analysis indicates that the detection does not rest on blinking alone and is consistent with a load-related pupil response. The post-hoc contrasts point the same way: with speaking held constant, time pressure was barely detectable, so this dataset cannot separate mental load from speech.

Limits on this study’s claims: This study investigates whether eye-tracking features are able to discriminate between COLET’s A1 and A4 task conditions when using participant-disjoint training. The within-subjects procedure uses the recordings of each participant of all four tasks for normalization purposes. The results do not prove real-time performance, cold start performance by this procedure, or speech-free detection of cognitive load. Rankings of the models diverged in terms of directionality with the use of both normalized and raw features analysis.
## LIMITATIONS
•	The high-load condition includes speaking, which raises the blink rate [23] and, in these data, increased tracking loss, so the full-feature results combine mental load with speech effects. Blinking followed speaking rather than time pressure (Table 17). In post-hoc comparisons, time pressure was detected only weakly when both activities involved speaking (A3 versus A4, ROC-AUC 0.60–0.66) and moderately when neither did (A1 versus A2, 0.68–0.77; Table 16); with 44 participants these intervals are wide.

**Table 17. Median blink rate and invalid samples per activity (44 participants).**

| **Activity** | **A1** | **A2** | **A3** | **A4** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined | undefined | undefined |
| Speaking | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| Time pressure | No | Yes | No | Yes |
| Blink rate (per minute) | 1.7 | 0.0 | 11.7 | 11.7 |
| Invalid samples | 0.9% | 0.7% | 6.9% | 6.9% |

•	The three excluded recordings all came from counting activities (P06 A3, P06 A4 and P17 A4), so the retained participants may be the ones who were easier to track while talking.

•	No equivalence margin was set before the analysis, so the model comparison can show only that no difference was detected, not that the two models perform equally.

•	The 45°/s velocity threshold was adopted from COLET and was not validated for this tracker; no threshold sensitivity analysis was run.

•	The permutation and shuffled-label tests used untuned models and test only label leakage. Without per-person standardization, ROC-AUC fell to 0.853–0.881 in P1 and 0.611–0.649 in P2, so the results depend on calibration against each person’s own recordings.

•	The pupil-only analysis is not fully independent of speaking, because the tracker re-fitted its pupil model more often in the counting activities.

•	Per-person standardization uses each participant’s own unlabeled recordings and relies on the balanced design; a deployed system would need a calibration session. Post hoc, A2-baseline centering, which keeps the classified recordings out of the reference, gave ROC-AUC 0.90–0.92 in P1; A2 involves time pressure and is not a neutral rest recording.

•	The choice between the ten-feature set and the five-feature fallback was made with the event-detection sanity check on all participants, so held-out data influenced that decision; it is an unsupervised quality check and does not use the labels.

•	Blinks and short tracking gaps can split fixations; because segments shorter than 55 ms are discarded, this may raise or lower fixation counts in the activity with more blinks, and the effect was not quantified.

•	Blink events were taken from the tracker’s own blink detector and were not validated independently; part of the higher blink rate in the counting activities may reflect tracking loss while talking.

•	Features are computed over whole activities, and A4 recordings were usually longer than A1 (median 51 vs 37 s). Rates are normalized by time, but recording length may affect how stable or representative the standard-deviation features (gaze spread and pupil standard deviation) are.

•	The puzzle images differ in brightness and no stimulus-luminance correction was applied; the COLET authors’ check [18] suggests a small effect, but it was not re-tested here.

•	The sample is small (44 participants, 88 samples) and comes from a laboratory task with a chin rest, which limits generalization to other people and settings.

•	In the released data, two participant IDs (P28 and P31) hold the same eye recordings; the recordings were kept once, but it cannot be determined whose they are.

•	Only the two extreme activities were classified in the main analysis, so the results do not show how well finer load levels could be distinguished.

•	The released data do not give the order of the activities. Inferred post hoc from the recording timestamps, the order varied between participants (A4 followed A1 for 18 of 44), and neither model’s predicted probabilities were related to the position of the activity (all p ≥ 0.19). Fixation rate rose slightly with position (Holm-corrected p = 0.024), so a small practice or fatigue effect on this feature cannot be ruled out.

•	The robustness analyses in Chapter 4 and Appendix B were added after the main results had been seen and were not corrected for multiple comparisons. Except for A2-baseline centering, they use the same standardization over all four activities as the main analysis.
## RECOMMENDATIONS
For future research, the following are recommended:

1.	Repeat the comparison on a dataset whose high-load condition does not involve speaking, for example a silent working-memory task, to separate mental load from speech effects.

2.	Classify A1 versus A3 and A2 versus A4 in COLET, which differ only in speaking, to complete the comparison of speaking and time pressure begun in the post-hoc analyses and to measure the speech effect directly.

3.	Evaluate calibration from a separate, neutral baseline recording, since the unstandardized analysis showed that per-person standardization accounts for much of the reported performance and the post-hoc A2 baseline still involved time pressure.

4.	Handle pupil-model refits explicitly, for example by computing pupil features per stable model segment.

5.	Extend the work to more than two load levels and to real-time detection on shorter time windows once a suitable dataset is available.

For practitioners who want interpretable workload monitoring from eye tracking, Logistic Regression on a small set of well-established features (blink rate, pupil size and fixation rate) is a reasonable candidate for tasks like the one studied here, which involve speaking under time pressure, provided that each user’s data can be standardized against their own baseline. Silent high-load tasks were examined only post hoc (A1 versus A2, ROC-AUC 0.68–0.77), and the blink effect may go the other way there: in these data the median blink rate fell from 1.7 per minute in A1 to 0.0 in A2, the silent time-pressure activity, and visual tasks are known to reduce blinking [36]. This should be checked first (Recommendation 1).

# APPENDIX A. XGBOOST GAIN IMPORTANCE (P1)
Gain importance is the average improvement in the training objective when a feature is used for a split. It is reported here for completeness only, because built-in tree importance measures can be biased towards certain features; the main importance results in Chapter 4 use SHAP and permutation importance. Values are averaged over the 44 leave-one-participant-out folds.

**Table A1.** XGBoost gain importance in P1.

| **Feature** | **Mean gain** | **SD** | **Folds in which the feature was used** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined | undefined |
| Blink rate | 8.09 | 3.35 | 44 |
| Saccade rate | 3.57 | 2.91 | 44 |
| Pupil diameter, mean | 2.33 | 1.50 | 44 |
| Fixation rate | 1.49 | 0.93 | 44 |
| Fixation duration | 1.19 | 1.02 | 42 |
| Saccade amplitude | 0.69 | 0.61 | 40 |

# APPENDIX B. POST-HOC WINDOWED ANALYSIS
This analysis was added after the main results had been seen and was not part of the pre-specified plan. Each retained recording was cut into non-overlapping 10 s windows by gaze timestamp, and the shorter remainder at the end was dropped. The window length is the researchers’ own choice; it is limited by activities that last under 40 s. Features were computed on each window with the same code as the main analysis, and windows with more than 35% invalid samples were excluded (9 in A3 and 11 in A4). Per-person standardization used each participant’s windows from all four activities. The models were evaluated on 153 A1 and 230 A4 windows from all 44 participants with the same nested leave-one-participant-out procedure, so no participant’s windows were in both the training and the test data. Because the two classes are unequal in size, balanced accuracy is reported alongside ROC-AUC.

**Table B1.** Windowed analysis, A1 versus A4 (10 s windows).

| **Features** | **Standardized** | **Logistic Regression ROC-AUC (95% CI)** | **XGBoost ROC-AUC (95% CI)** | **Balanced accuracy, LR / XGBoost** | **XGBoost − LR (95% CI)** |
| undefined | undefined | undefined | undefined | undefined | undefined |
| P1 | Yes | 0.928 (0.893–0.958) | 0.901 (0.851–0.943) | 0.855 / 0.844 | −0.027 (−0.049 to −0.009) |
| P2 | Yes | 0.829 (0.738–0.906) | 0.825 (0.740–0.899) | 0.750 / 0.782 | −0.005 (−0.029 to 0.023) |
| P1 | No | 0.819 (0.765–0.874) | 0.806 (0.752–0.862) | 0.761 / 0.741 | −0.014 (−0.054 to 0.023) |
| P2 | No | 0.626 (0.573–0.693) | 0.621 (0.570–0.671) | 0.513 / 0.570 | −0.005 (−0.054 to 0.037) |

The pattern of the main analysis held at window level: performance was high with standardization, lower without it, and lower with pupil features only. ROC-AUC was lower than with whole activities, as expected because a 10 s window holds few blinks [23]. With all standardized features, Logistic Regression was slightly but significantly better than XGBoost (difference −0.027, 95% CI −0.049 to −0.009). The standardization still uses each participant’s own windows.
